title: Why archives keep the awkward records

segments.text: Digitising an archive is often described as an act of preservation. The phrase is accurate, but incomplete. A scan protects a page from handling, while a catalogue makes it easier to find; neither decision is neutral. Someone has still decided what is worth scanning and how it should be described.

This problem becomes especially visible in collections assembled by institutions with a clear public image. Their official reports may be carefully organised, whereas complaints, drafts and marginal notes are scattered through boxes.

The scattered material is inconvenient, but it may be the most revealing. It records hesitation and disagreement, which polished documents tend to remove. Researchers can then compare what an organisation said about itself with the decisions it was actually considering.

Digital tools can help with that comparison. A search may reveal a repeated phrase across decades, or connect a name in a letter with an unrelated administrative file. Such connections are invitations to investigate, not conclusions delivered by the software.
The archive therefore needs two kinds of care. It needs technical care, so files remain readable, and intellectual care, so descriptions admit uncertainty and gaps.
This second form of care is easy to underestimate because it produces no visible interface. Its effect is a record that can be questioned rather than merely searched.
Preservation, in this broader sense, does not freeze the past. It keeps open the possibility of discovering that the first account was incomplete.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every archive contains a chain of such decisions, beginning with the material that was kept and continuing through arrangement, selection and description. Digitisation adds another link to that chain rather than removing it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: For that reason, archivists increasingly value records that appear unfinished. Their lack of polish is not a defect when the aim is to understand how choices were made.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The technology is most useful when it leaves the researcher with a sharper question. Its speed can widen the field of evidence, but interpretation still depends on context and comparison.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Not every file deserves the same priority. Some are fragile, some are frequently requested and others offer a rare view of people who were absent from the institution’s formal narrative.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A catalogue can make the omissions harder to see if it presents its categories as natural. Clear labels are valuable, but they should not conceal the judgement behind them.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The same caution applies to search results. Finding a word is not the same as understanding why it was used, or what was left unsaid around it.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: One collection includes a set of photographs whose glass plates required a special temperature before they could be handled safely.

questions.prompt: Which paragraph explains that digitisation adds to existing selection decisions?
questions.explanation: It develops the opening claim that preservation decisions are not neutral.

questions.prompt: Which paragraph refers to the value of records that are not polished?
questions.explanation: It links unfinished records with understanding how choices were made.

questions.prompt: Which paragraph explains the proper role of digital tools?
questions.explanation: It says technology widens evidence and sharpens questions, while interpretation remains human and contextual.

questions.prompt: Which paragraph warns that categories can hide judgement?
questions.explanation: It directly says a catalogue can conceal the judgement behind its labels.

questions.prompt: Which paragraph identifies two different priorities for selecting material?
questions.explanation: It lists fragility, demand and representation as reasons for different priorities.

questions.prompt: Which paragraph cautions against treating a search result as an explanation?
questions.explanation: It distinguishes finding a word from understanding its context and omissions.
